prime.problem: Once attention and experts sit on different GPUs, each token goes attention → network → experts → network → attention on every layer. With one batch, every GPU idles while the other side works and while data is on the wire.
prime.fits: Second MegaScale-Infer card. Part I split the pools and sized n_a; this card keeps both pools busy with the pipeline card's micro-batch trick in a two-stage, per-layer form, and replaces NCCL for the many-to-many traffic. The results close the MoE block.
expect: the three constraints: T_a ≈ T_e, T_c < T_f, m ≥ 2(1 + T_c/T_f)
M2N: a CPU-driven RDMA path instead of NCCL
results with named baselines, and Step-3's latency critique
prime.goal: Pick the number of micro-batches for a given compute and network time, predict the busy share and the per-token latency cost, and read the paper's multipliers against their baselines.

attend: Why is m = 2 never quite enough when the network time is non-zero?
What does each of the three constraints hide: the other side's compute, or the network?
Why does the ping-pong pipeline raise throughput but leave per-token latency the same or worse?
Which NCCL behaviours make it slow for this M-to-N traffic at ~200 KB messages?
Why is "up to 1.90×" a different claim from "7.11×", and which baseline is each against?

must: A micro-batch's round trip is T_a + T_c + T_e + T_c = 2(T_f + T_c) when balanced → a node has m·T_f of other work meanwhile → no idle time if m·T_f ≥ 2(T_f + T_c) → m ≥ 2(1 + T_c/T_f): 3 when T_c < ½T_f, 4 for slower networks, and m = 2 always leaves a gap

Balance (T_a ≈ T_e) removes one side waiting on the other → a fast link (T_c < T_f) lets the transfer hide under compute → enough micro-batches cover the round trip → break any one and busy share drops (T_e = T_a/2: experts 49.7%; T_c = 1.3 T_f: 64.6%, even m = 8 only 76.5%)

Each micro-batch waits for m slots of work at every layer → per-token latency ≤ m·T_f·L → at a 150 ms TBT SLO, Mixtral's 56 layers and m = 3 leave T_f ≤ 893 µs per layer → throughput per GPU rises, latency doesn't fall → a loose SLO is part of the recipe (Step-3's critique)

Small per-pair messages (~196 KB for Mixtral) make fixed per-message overheads dominate → NCCL's GPU→CPU-proxy copies, ≤ 8-op groups and synchronisation push T_c toward T_f → a CPU-driven RDMA path with no copies or SMs: 4.2× throughput, 68.2% lower median and 92.9% lower P99 at 256 KB, M = N = 8
elevated: Fixed micro-batch size means throughput ∝ busy share → the model predicts m 1→2 ≈ 1.99× and 2→3 ≈ 1.2–1.4×; the paper measured 1.9× and 1.10–1.38× (bigger models gain more because they communicate more)
reference: Eq 6's per-GPU communication formula and Eq 8's memory bound
Algorithm 1's loop bounds (M ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8}, N_m = 4) and the "minimize" typo
the 1.7× vs 1.86× heterogeneous discrepancy and the production 1.5–2.0×

compress.prompt: Write the three constraints from memory, each followed by → and what it hides. Then derive m ≥ 2(1 + T_c/T_f) in two lines and write the latency bound. Finish with one sentence on why NCCL was replaced.
checklist: T_a ≈ T_e hides one side's compute from the other
T_c < T_f lets the transfer fit under a micro-batch's compute
m·T_f ≥ 2(T_f + T_c) covers one round trip, so m ≥ 2(1 + T_c/T_f): 3 or 4
per-token latency grows to about m·T_f·L; throughput, not speed, improves
NCCL's copies, grouping and sync overheads dominate small M2N messages

retrieve.q: Explain why the ping-pong pipeline needs at least 3 micro-batches on a fast network but 4 on a slower one.
answer: a micro-batch's round trip is 2(T_f + T_c): its own compute on both sides plus two transfers
the node must have m·T_f of other work to cover it
m ≥ 2(1 + T_c/T_f): below T_c = ½T_f that's ≤ 3, above it up to 4 (T_c/T_f < 1)

retrieve.q: Walk through the first few time units of the m = 3 timeline with T_a = T_e = 1 and T_c = 0.4: when each micro-batch starts attention, when it reaches the experts, and whether the attention node ever waits.
answer: micro-batch 1 arrives at the experts at 1.4 and finishes at 2.4, and is back at 2.8
the attention node frees up at 3.0, just after micro-batch 1 returns, so it runs back to back
with m = 2 it would free up at 2.0 and wait until 2.8

retrieve.q: A chat product needs a 50 ms TBT on a 56-layer MoE. What per-layer compute time does m = 3 allow, and what does that tell you about using MegaScale-Infer's design as-is?
answer: T_f ≤ 50 ms ÷ (3 × 56) ≈ 298 µs per layer (vs 893 µs at 150 ms)
that forces much smaller micro-batches or faster GPUs, cutting the throughput gain
Step-3 redesigned the model and pipeline (3 stages, ~272 µs per layer per stage) to use AFD under 50 ms

retrieve.q: Why did MegaScale-Infer's own M2N library add up to 1.53× on top of the NCCL-based disaggregated version?
answer: with NCCL, T_c approached T_f, breaking constraint 2, so the network stopped hiding
the CPU-driven RDMA path removes GPU→CPU copies, group setup and GPU synchronisation
with T_c < T_f the ping-pong pipeline can hide the transfer again

compare.q: The serving pipeline (PP stages over layers) vs the ping-pong pipeline (two alternating pools per layer): what is the same trick, what is different about the stages, and how does each fail?
answer: both keep several micro-batches in flight so no stage waits
PP's stages are blocks of layers visited once per token; ping-pong's two stages alternate L times per token, with a network hop each way
PP fails on imbalanced micro-batches (prefill next to decode); ping-pong fails on unbalanced T_a/T_e or a slow link (T_c ≥ T_f)

compare.q: DeepEP's GPU-driven low-latency all-to-all vs MegaScale-Infer's CPU-driven M2N: which design choice does each make about who posts the network operations, and when does each win?
answer: DeepEP posts RDMA from the GPU (with a receive hook that overlaps without SMs)
M2N posts from CPU threads, argued to saturate the NIC at several hundred KB per pair
M2N suits AFD's larger per-pair messages; the paper concedes GPU-driven sends may win as messages get smaller with more experts

predict.q: Keep m = 3 and T_a = T_e, but the network slows to T_c/T_f = 0.7. What steady-state busy share does the model predict, and what should the planner do? Commit first.
predict.answer: Steady state is min(1, m / 2(1 + r)) = 3 / 3.4 ≈ 88%. Constraint 3 now needs m ≥ 3.4, so the planner should move to m = 4 (bound 3.4 ≤ 4), accepting a higher per-token latency (m·T_f·L grows by a third), or cut T_c with a better transfer path.

apply.task: Run labs/pingpong.py. Then compute by hand: (1) the smallest m for T_c/T_f = 0.45 and for 0.95; (2) Eq 5's T_total for Mixtral (L = 56) at m = 4, T_a = T_e = 1, T_c = 0.4, and compare with the lab; (3) the per-layer T_f budget at a 150 ms TBT for m = 4. Finally sweep T_e from 0.3 to 1.5 at T_a = 1 in the lab and describe which side idles on each end.
apply.done: You have two minimum-m values, a T_total that matches the lab, a per-layer budget, and a two-sentence description of the T_e sweep.
apply.hint: (1) 2 × 1.45 = 2.9 → m = 3; 2 × 1.95 = 3.9 → m = 4. (2) (1 + 1 + 2 × 0.4) + 1 × (4 × 56 − 1) = 2.8 + 223 = 225.8. (3) 150 ms ÷ (4 × 56) ≈ 670 µs. Sweep: T_e < 1 means experts idle (attention-bound, like DBRX at DP 1–4); T_e > 1 means attention idles (expert-bound, DBRX past DP 8).

Could you derive the m bound from the round trip without looking?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: m → throughput, or m → per-token latency?
